title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Are randomized classical and entanglement-assisted quantum communication polynomially related for every total Boolean function? Precisely, do universal constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that \[R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\le C\bigl(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1\bigr)^k\] for every pair of nonempty finite sets \(X,Y\) and every function \(F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\)?
why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

progress.text: The revised AND-functions paper proves the restricted \(O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*})^7\log^2 n)\) deterministic bound while explicitly retaining the general Log-Equivalence Conjecture.
Hasegawa–Le Gall report polynomial separations using constant-round quantum communication. The claimed advantage does not exceed every polynomial.

context_blocks.text: Communication complexity isolates the information that must cross between two parties who already have unlimited ability to process their own inputs. A quantum advantage in this setting is therefore a saving in transmitted information, rather than a faster local computation. The shared entanglement in the quantum model is a free, input-independent resource.

For a total function, every combination of an Alice input and a Bob input must be handled. Promise problems may omit difficult combinations, and relations may accept several different answers. These distinctions prevent the known much larger advantages for those models from automatically providing a counterexample here.

The polynomial has to be the same for all functions. Examples in which the classical cost is a fixed power of the quantum cost are compatible with the conjecture, even if that power exceeds two. The negation requires advantages that defeat every fixed polynomial bound.

Bhattacharya and coauthors state this as the Log-Equivalence Conjecture, attributed to Shi and Zhu. Their 2026 paper explicitly retains the general total-function question and studies a restricted composed family.

For \(F(x,y)=f(x_1\land y_1,\ldots,x_n\land y_n)\), their revised Theorem 1.2 gives \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}(F)=O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F))^7\log^2 n)\), where \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}\) denotes exact deterministic communication. The restriction to AND composition and the remaining \(\log^2 n\) factor keep this from being the stated universal polynomial in quantum cost alone.

Hasegawa and Le Gall’s August 2026 preprint obtains a polynomial quantum advantage for a total function using a constant number of quantum communication rounds. Its improvement concerns interaction: the size of the communication gap remains polynomial. It therefore does not refute the general polynomial-relation conjecture.

Resolving the conjecture would determine whether total Boolean communication imposes a general limit on quantum savings. The comparison permits arbitrary prior entanglement and unrestricted interaction, so such a limit would apply beyond particular algorithms or graph-like compositions.

answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal polynomial bound or of its negation. A negative answer must show that for every \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\), some finite total Boolean function satisfies \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)>C(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1)^k\). A superpolynomial separating family can witness this; one fixed polynomial separation cannot. A bound with an extra input-length factor, a promise-problem or relation separation, or a comparison imposing a fixed round limit does not resolve the stated all-functions, unrestricted-round target.
definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and Bob must output \(F(x,y)\). A protocol is agreed in advance for the entire function \(F\). Local computation and storage are unrestricted and free; only communication is charged. The protocol may depend on \(F\), but its shared resources are independent of the actual inputs. In the classical model the parties exchange bits and may use shared public randomness and private randomness. In the quantum model they exchange qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may start with any finite-dimensional shared entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). There is no fixed upper bound on the amount of this prior entanglement; its preparation is not charged. Local quantum operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, with measurement outcomes retained in local registers, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Classical bits sent by a quantum protocol count as transmitted qubits. Neither model receives free input-dependent advice or any communication through timing, message length, silence or postselection. One may use a fixed finite alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused transmissions; local branches cannot signal through the schedule. Arbitrarily many rounds are allowed, with no input-length-dependent round restriction imposed by the question. The cost is the worst-case total number of bits or qubits transmitted, including all rounds and all randomness or measurement branches. In either model the output must equal \(F(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every pair \((x,y)\). The quantities \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\) and \(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)\) are the least costs among protocols with this guarantee. Total means that all of \(X\times Y\) is the correctness domain; no additional joint promise is allowed. The additive one in the polynomial handles zero-communication functions. The constants \(C,k\) must be independent of the function, the domains, any bit encoding of the inputs, and the amount of shared entanglement.

importance.reason: A general classical-versus-quantum comparison across all total communication problems, with a sharp distinction from promise-problem separations.

sentences: Two parties must evaluate a Boolean function when each holds one part of the input.
The question asks whether randomized classical communication is polynomially bounded by quantum communication with shared entanglement for every total function.
Both models allow bounded error on each input, and their costs count transmitted bits or qubits rather than local computation.
A positive answer would limit quantum communication advantages whenever the function is defined on every input pair.
The totality condition is central: results for promise problems cannot be substituted, and the polynomial must be universal across all finite domains.
